justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a mildly bullish baseline assumption across all three horizons. For the one-day estimate, I anchored closely to the prevailing price level, assuming mean-reversion tendencies and modest continuation of recent momentum would dominate over such a short window. The one-week estimate edges slightly higher, reflecting a weak upward drift consistent with the broader trend, while acknowledging that short-term noise could easily overwhelm any directional signal. The one-month estimate pushes modestly further to the upside, incorporating a longer-run growth assumption while remaining humble about compounding uncertainty over that timeframe. In all cases, I was essentially assuming no major structural break and a continuation of the recent trading environment.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated to reflect the scaling of uncertainty with time. Over one day, realized volatility tends to be relatively contained, so the interval is narrow. Over one week, intraday noise accumulates and macro data releases, earnings surprises, or sentiment shifts can meaningfully alter direction, widening the band considerably. Over one month, the range expands further still, as any number of macro regime changes, policy shifts, or sector-specific developments can compound. I also factored in that implied volatility in options markets tends to embed a premium above realized volatility, suggesting the market itself prices in fatter tails than recent calm might suggest.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions — an unexpected inflation print, a central bank surprise, geopolitical escalation, or a credit event — could produce sharp drawdowns that breach the lower bound of even my one-month interval. On the upside, a positive catalyst such as a strong earnings beat, a dovish policy pivot, or a sector-driven momentum surge could push prices above my upper bounds faster than anticipated. Liquidity conditions also matter: in thin markets, moves can overshoot fundamentals significantly in either direction before correcting.

Finally, I want to acknowledge that my intervals, while wide by conventional standards, still implicitly assume some degree of stationarity in the underlying process. Tail events — genuine structural breaks, flash crashes, or black swan developments — are by definition underrepresented in historical data and could render even my widest bounds inadequate. Forecasting at a one-month horizon in particular should be treated with significant humility, as the compounding of uncertainty means the true distribution of outcomes is likely heavier-tailed than any symmetric confidence interval cleanly captures.
